item.title: Israeli Settlers Turn a Palestinian Rite Into a Gantlet of Violence and Fear
item.description:
The families had only just begun harvesting olives when the attack started. Clad in all black, bearing metal batons and guns, Israeli settlers materialized without warning.

Ilham Al-Bazari, one of the Palestinians farming, froze. It was too late to run, she said.

Her husband was shot in the leg, and settlers attacked her teenage nephew. Believing they might spare a 50-year-old woman, Mrs. Al-Bazari said she jumped on top of her nephew to protect him. They broke her arm instead.

Her cousin, Ali Al-Bazari, an off-duty captain in the Palestinian Authority’s security forces, raced to help and was shot in the back by a settler.

The Israeli military showed up shortly after, Mrs. Al-Bazari and other witnesses said, as her cousin lay on the ground dying.

“We called on the soldiers to allow an ambulance,” she said. “But they refused.”

Mr. Al-Bazari, 44, died on Oct. 7, the first person killed in this year’s harvest — the most violent olive season in recent history, still weeks from ending. The Israeli military did not respond to requests for comment about Mr. Al-Bazari’s case or other incidents described by Palestinians or seen by journalists from The New York Times.

The violence of this year’s harvest is a distillation of the turmoil upending Palestinian life in the Israeli-occupied West Bank since the Hamas-led attacks of Oct. 7, 2023, which killed as many as 1,200 Israelis. As the country plunged into war in Gaza, Israeli settler expansion sharply accelerated in the West Bank, as extremist settlers — Jewish Israelis living in areas that Israel occupied in the 1967 Arab-Israeli war — push Palestinians off the land by intimidation and force.

Each year, the olive harvest has grown more tense but endured as both a social and economic rite for Palestinians. Families gather in groves, serving coffee brewed over open fires as several generations pick olives together. As many as 100,000 families rely on revenue generated by the harvest, which typically runs from mid-October to mid-November, Palestinian officials say.

In the last three weeks alone, armed Israeli settlers have launched hundreds of attacks, according to the Israeli rights group Yesh Din, the United Nations and the Palestinian Authority. Settlers have lit trees ablaze, shot farmers and bludgeoned men, women and children. On Friday, Palestinian gunmen opened fire on Israelis: The Israeli military said that two soldiers and two Palestinian assailants were killed.

In at least three instances witnessed by The Times in the past week — in the villages of Khirbet Abu Falah, Turmus Ayya and Deir Abu Masha’al — soldiers stood by as settlers stopped Palestinians from harvesting olives.

The far-right government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has vigorously supported settlers seeking to redraw the map of the West Bank. It has also allowed extremist settlers to operate with near impunity, even as violence has soared ahead of Israeli elections that could determine Mr. Netanyahu’s political fate.

Entire communities sit empty, residents run off by marauding settlers who have established more than 100 outposts over the last three years and are rarely stopped by Israeli troops. Hundreds of prominent Israelis, including former top-ranked military and intelligence officials, have accused Mr. Netanyahu’s government of allowing what they describe as ethnic cleansing.

Mr. Netanyahu’s office has rejected those accusations. Asked for comment about settler violence, an office spokesman, Doron Spielman, said: “While there is Jewish crime, it is not state-sponsored or state-supported. It is condemned; people are arrested and brought to court, and if they are found guilty, they are prosecuted.”

Three Palestinians have been killed in recent weeks, one during an olive harvest, with many others wounded and trees destroyed. A series of exceptionally brazen attacks have drawn condemnation from U.S. and other officials, some of whom have called them acts of terrorism.

In one attack last week, settlers assaulted European officials on a visit to a Christian village. In another, they badly beat a 63-year-old photojournalist from The Washington Post, breaking two of her ribs and fracturing several vertebrae.

Then, on Wednesday, a delegation of rabbis joined by several Americans, including Brad Lander, a Democratic nominee for U.S. Congress, were detained by Israeli authorities while accompanying Palestinian farmers near Bethlehem. The Israeli military said they were detained because of “the security risk posed by conducting an uncoordinated harvest near an Israeli community.”

Military aggression has also sharply increased in the West Bank: the Israeli military have killed more than 1,100 Palestinians in the last three years, a sum greater than the previous 17 years combined, according to U.N. data, a figure that includes combatants.

In many cases, the soldiers appear to protect their fellow Israelis while detaining the Palestinians who come under attack.

The Israeli military has rejected accusations that it supports “the actions of violent groups” in the West Bank. It says its mission is to “protect all residents,” and that any soldier who takes part in settler attacks or stands by while they occur is “acting in complete disregard” of their orders.

“The season is not starting off well,” said Ramez Obeid, head of the Palestinian Agriculture Ministry’s olives department. “We estimate 50 percent of the land will be inaccessible.”

Indeed, as settlers paralyze harvesting, some communities like the village of Jalud can barely harvest enough to produce oil for themselves.

Jalud and its surrounding areas stretch between several hills, nearly all of which have become home to new settler outposts since 2023. The settlers’ presence has made accessing more than 1,000 acres along the village’s periphery impossible.

“They stole my equipment just a few meters away from our home,” said Raed Al-Naser, the mayor. “And they are doing this to many others.”

Fearing for their lives, residents let the olives hang from trees, untouched.

Except where the settlers take them.

“It’s not the olive harvest season,” said the mayor. “It’s the olive stealing season.”

The attacks typically follow a pattern and are executed with precision, as Palestinians described them and as we saw ourselves.

Settlers have claimed the high ground in much of the West Bank, placing encampments above the olive groves that terrace up and down the limestone bluffs.

From the ground below, one can see the settlers preparing, usually dressed in black hoodies with masks and armed with rifles and other weapons.

They descend with speed, sometimes on foot, fanning out across the groves and hiding among the trees. In other cases, they barrel down roads into the lower ground.

This was the case in Khirbet Abu Falah last Friday, when 50 or 60 settlers laid siege to farmers harvesting crops before a group assaulted the veteran Post photographer. Mr. Netanyahu’s office said the “facts surrounding the confrontation” were being investigated.

Where they can, Palestinian lookouts scale unclaimed hillsides so they can warn their neighbors about attacks. Without them, the farmers would have no chance to flee before the settlers came storming down, like what happened with Mr. Al-Bazari.

By Israeli law, Palestinian villagers cannot be armed. Even throwing rocks at settlers could land a Palestinian in prison, often meaning that the only recourse available is to flee their own lands.

On Monday in Turmus Ayya, a Palestinian village filled with the homes of dual U.S. citizens, settlers attacked one such house while its owners were out harvesting olives.

We arrived after the assault began. Settlers burned cars, smashed a neighbor’s windows and beat an American citizen to the point of hospitalization, his family said. In the aftermath, we saw Israeli soldiers threaten the Palestinians outside of the home with tear gas if they did not disperse.

“But this is where I live,” said one Palestinian man, in English. “Where is your warrant saying we must leave our own lands?”

“For the Palestinians, we don’t need a warrant,” the soldier said. “We can just tell you to go.”

Everyone pressed inside the destroyed home, where glass crunched underfoot.

Hanan Mousa Hamayel, who was inside during the attack, shouted in despair.

“How long will it be like this?” she asked, adding, “We live in fear 24 hours. We cannot find peace even in our own homes.”

In some cases, the mere threat of violence and the apparent complicity between settlers and soldiers was enough to halt the harvest.

We saw this in the village of Deir Abu Masha’al on Monday morning, when a farmer, Mahmoud Rabia, arrived at his olive fields to find a half dozen settlers already there.

Mr. Rabia, 60, expected the worst as he trundled into his grove, and the fear was palpable as settlers walked among the farmers, despite the presence of journalists and Israeli activists trying to help the farmers. A young settler jumped into an SUV, using it to block the road back to the village.

The crowd braced for an attack as four more settlers walked up the road to join the others.

And then the army showed up.

Only it wasn’t to push the settlers off the private land; it was to evict everyone else.

The soldiers forced the farmers and others away, brandishing a military order closing the zone. The settlers stood around laughing and smiling.

As one farmer attempted to drive away, another young settler jumped in front of his car to stop him. He told an officer to arrest him, claiming the Palestinian had attacked him. The military detained the man.

The boy then called out another Palestinian for holding a hand saw, and soldiers detained him, too.

Mr. Rabia fumed.

“My ancestors farmed this land,” he said. “And I have harvested these trees through the intifadas, through hard times and violent times.”

Through it all, he had never been kept from his own land.

“I don’t care if they have their outposts,” he said. “I just want them to leave me be.”

item.title: Iran in ‘Advanced Stages’ of Planning Attacks Against Americans, Officials Say
item.description:
The U.S. government has put employees on heightened alert across the Middle East and moved to reduce personnel levels at embassies and consulates because of intelligence showing Iran is in the advanced stages of planning attacks against Americans, U.S. officials said on Friday.

Intelligence officials raised alarms to Secretary of State Marco Rubio in a memo on Friday that warned about the dangers to State Department employees in the Middle East and other regions, the officials said.

The memo, from Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, said that agencies had “received intelligence that Iran has substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel. The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against U.S. citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries.”

The Trump administration confirmed the memo on Friday night through a U.S. official. The move demonstrated the seriousness with which the U.S. government is taking the threat, officials said. Axios earlier reported on the memo.

U.S. agencies assess that the threat against Americans in the Middle East and several other countries is at the highest level since the start of the war in February, U.S. officials said.

President Trump and top aides have received regular briefings on the rising threats, which go beyond the Middle East, one official said. Analysts have been examining the intelligence on the threats to U.S. officials, including ambassadors, in the past three weeks. Some material indicates Iran may have operatives in the United States, the official said. The Iranian plans also include potential targets in Europe, U.S. officials said.

But another official cautioned that Iran’s ability to carry out attacks in the United States and other territories overseas is limited, and its ambitions to strike are greater than its capability to do so.

The White House did not reply to a request for comment. Mr. Clayton’s office and the C.I.A. declined to comment.

The State Department said through a U.S. official that “when it comes to our staffing at embassies, we constantly evaluate new information about the security environment.”

The official said that the threat of attacks by Houthi forces in Yemen and of “Iranian terror plots targeting U.S. officials” were informing State Department decisions on staffing adjustments for embassies. The missions were already at reduced levels under what the department calls “restricted operating status,” often invoked in conflict zones, the official said.

The alerts over the new threats come after eight months of a war against Iran started by Mr. Trump and Israel that has sent energy prices soaring, roiling economies around the world and eroding Mr. Trump’s approval at home. The United States and Israel have drawn up plans for a new wave of strikes on Iran after the U.S. midterm elections, though Mr. Trump has not made a final decision to carry them out, The New York Times reported on Wednesday.

Mr. Trump has refrained from ordering large-scale attacks on Iran in recent months, but the U.S. military has carried out a blockade of Iranian ports in an effort to keep Iran from selling oil and other energy products on the global market.

Iranian officials have sought different ways to strike back at the United States and its allies, U.S. officials said. In early October, the U.S. military took the extraordinary step of withdrawing all 12 B-1 Air Force bombers from a base in southern England because commanders had received information about Iranian threats to the installation, R.A.F. Fairford.

Mr. Clayton said in his memo to Mr. Rubio on Friday that he was seeking to downgrade the classification around some intelligence so that more U.S. government employees could be informed about what the memo’s subject line called the “lethal plotting against Americans in the Middle East and certain other countries.”

On Wednesday, the State Department ordered the departure of nonessential employees and their families from Saudi Arabia, Tommy Pigott, a department spokesman, said in a statement.

The agency has also been quietly moving personnel in and out of many of the other diplomatic missions in the region. It has designated almost all U.S. missions in the Middle East as being on “restricted operating status,” which gives the department more leeway to adjust staffing levels without putting out notifications.

The drawdown of diplomats and other U.S. government employees at the missions is a direct result of the recent intelligence about Iranian attack plans, U.S. officials said.

After the United States and Israel struck Iran on Feb. 28, the Iranian military retaliated by firing drones and missiles at Arab nations across the Middle East, as well as at Israel.

On March 2, the State Department issued a mandatory departure for nonessential employees at missions in Iraq, Jordan and Bahrain.

Around that time, the department also ordered nonessential personnel and their families in the missions in Saudi Arabia to leave the country because Iran had carried out attacks against the embassy in Riyadh, and on nearby areas.

In the run-up to the war, only two embassies said employees could go on so-called authorized departure, which meant nonessential personnel and family members could leave if they wanted to do so. Those were the embassy in Beirut, which issued the message four days before the war began, and the embassy in Jerusalem, which did so the day before the start of the war.

During periods this summer when the violence ebbed, the State Department told some diplomats they could return to their posts.

The State Department came under intense criticism for not urging the many thousands of U.S. citizens in the region to leave before the start of the war, and for providing limited help to evacuate them once the missiles began flying. The Trump administration and Israel had secretly been planning strikes for many weeks before the start of the assault.

item.title: How Defiant Youth Are Testing India’s Idea of Democracy
item.description:
India’s democracy is facing its biggest test in a half-decade. Its signals are worth watching at a time of democratic backsliding in so many corners of the world.

A defiant generation of young Indians has poured into the streets on and off for the past four months — first over education, then over voting rights. They did so at a time when dissent was all but crushed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s near-total hold on power, confronting the government over some of the most fundamental principles of democracy: the right to vote, the right to ask questions of those in power and the right to protest. They were irreverent and funny, and they appealed to India’s prized tradition of democracy — some waving the national flag as they were hauled away by police.

For now, at least, their street revolt has ebbed, thanks in part to an extraordinary show of force by state security organs. Still, after more than a decade of democratic backsliding in India, their defiance has broken the dam, unleashing the hopes and fury of a generation in the world’s largest democracy.

“The fear needs to go,” Gul Kumaria, 26, told me at a recent rally called by the Cockroach Janta Party, the Gen Z movement that catalyzed this year’s youth rebellion. It was a sentiment I heard repeatedly from young Indians on the streets.

India’s youth-led protests are driven by many of the same grievances fueling protests in Europe: poor schools, a paucity of jobs, a lack of government accountability, and a loss of faith in traditional institutions. But they have differed in one crucial way. They have been largely nonviolent.

Democracy can be a potent rallying cry.

Mr. Modi, speaking to an international business conference in New Delhi in mid-October, called India “the mother of democracy.” Members of his ruling Bharatiya Janata Party described opposition politicians as sore losers in democratic elections and inveighed against what they called anarchy on the streets. The defense minister, Rajnath Singh, last week accused opponents of trying to topple the government with what he called a “politics of disruption.”

The protesters swiftly clapped back with their own appeals to democracy.

“But demanding answers from the govt is not anarchy, protesting against injustice on the streets is not anarchy, and questioning those who hold public office is certainly not anarchy,” the cockroach movement’s 31-year-old founder, Abhijeet Dipke, retorted in a social media post. “These are the most fundamental expressions of democracy.”

Neha Bora, a leader from the youth wing of one of India’s communist parties, called the B.J.P. “the enemy of democracy.”

Rahul Gandhi, the opposition Indian National Congress party leader, seized on the same language. “We are fighting together to restore democratic rule, genuine democratic rule in this country,” he said, with Mx. Bora at his side. His party has flailed in elections for over a decade.

Not since then-Prime Minister Indira Gandhi, who was Mr. Gandhi’s grandmother, imposed emergency rule in June 1975 has India faced such a reckoning over its most prized tradition.

The cockroaches energized India’s young this summer over a dysfunctional college entrance exam system. They were playful and often cocky, and they used Instagram reels to draw in people who hadn’t been politically active before. They created what Milan Vaishnav, South Asia director at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, called “viral symbols of dissent.”

“Humor and satire are underrated political weapons,” he said.

Except the cockroaches lacked the organizing skills of India’s robust leftist student movements. They called protests only to get locked up before they could lead them, which is when the young communists like Mx. Bora stepped up. They organized pop-up protests. They gave the police the runaround. They held on to each other so tightly it was hard for police to pry them apart. They sprinted from security forces, jumped over barricades and crawled out of police bus windows.

Together, the newbie cockroaches and the more experienced communists created an opening that the established opposition parties had not had in over a decade.

Only after the youth took to the streets did Mr. Gandhi’s Congress party — founded more than 140 years ago to oppose British rule — mobilize street protests of its own. Three days after the cockroach protests were squelched by police, Congress brought thousands of its supporters to the center of Delhi. Police let the march proceed.

Whether these legacy politicians can leverage the raw and rare defiance of India’s young people remains to be seen.

“There’s a sense of exhaustion and frustration with the existing structures of our polity, both the institutions and the political parties,” said Yamini Aiyar, the former president of a Delhi-based think tank, the Center for Policy Research, who is now a visiting professor at Brown University.

The cockroaches drew attention, she said, precisely because they were not an established political party. “That begs the question: What happens next, what does it mean for democracy that all its formal sites, formal institutions are seen as lacking credibility among the young who are taking to the streets and demanding accountability?”

At the heart of the current protests is the country’s election commission, which for most of India’s 79-year history since independence was trusted to run relatively free and fair elections. Its integrity has been severely dented by a sweeping revision of the voter roll that eliminated 130 million names and that critics saw as an effort to entrench B.J.P. rule.

Another target is the country’s judiciary. Once seen as a pillar of India’s feisty democracy, it has come under criticism in recent years for having become a tool of the ruling party to suppress its rivals.

The protests are putting pressure on the courts to uphold the rights enshrined in India’s Constitution.

If supporters of Mr. Modi have been swayed by a brand of right-wing Hindu nationalism, India’s youth protesters have appealed to a different kind of nationalism — one that valorizes their nation’s liberal traditions.

The cockroach movement leaders are fond of wearing T-shirts bearing the image of Mohandas K. Gandhi, India’s icon of nonviolent protest. They hold aloft copies of the Indian Constitution at rallies. They unfurl their nation’s tricolor flag — the tiranga in Hindi — in places where protests are banned.

“Waving the tiranga is not a crime,” Mr. Dipke, the cockroach movement’s founder, declared last week as he called on Indians to bring the flag to a park in central Delhi. “My tiranga is my pride.”

The police arrested him before he could get to the park. He raised the Indian flag as he was stuffed into a police car.

item.title: Alberta’s Referendum Was Clear, Unlike Danielle Smith’s Future
item.description:
Days after Albertans voted on their future within Canada, signs promoting both sides of the question are still lingering on the lawns of many homes — some of them mixed in with Halloween decorations. They aren’t the only things still hanging around from Premier Danielle Smith’s referendum.

The referendum result was decisive. As of Friday, the still-unofficial results showed that 75 percent of Albertans chose to remain Canadian. Just one-quarter of voters were seeking a second, binding referendum to secede from Canada.

[Read: Voters in Oil-Rich Alberta Reject Leaving Canada]

Predictably, many separatist leaders vowed to fight on, with some claiming they had fully expected defeat this time around.

Much less clear, however, is the future of Ms. Smith, the premier, and her United Conservative Party.

As I wrote before the vote, Ms. Smith managed to alienate people on both sides of the Canada question.

[Read: Alberta Voting on Its Future in Canada, With Its Leader Caught in the Middle]

Federalists were put off when she initially came to the aid of the separatists. After a court struck down their attempt to hold a direct referendum on independence, Ms. Smith added her question on staying or holding a second, binding vote as the 10th one on her previously announced referendum on constitutional powers and immigration.

Then Ms. Smith turned around and angered separatists, a group largely responsible for carrying her to office, by saying that she herself would vote to remain a part of Canada.

It didn’t end there. To the consternation of many on the side to stay, Ms. Smith didn’t require United Conservative members of the legislature to follow her lead and vote for a united Canada. While she was not invisible during the period leading up to the vote, many people viewed her campaigning for Canada as tepid.

“The premier hasn’t done, at all, much,” Thomas Lukaszuk, a former Progressive Conservative legislator and deputy premier who led the Forever Canadian group, told me days before the vote. “I had the pleasure, or honor, of serving with five premiers in the Alberta provincial government. And I can tell you, not one of those previous premiers would have ever asked Question 10.”

In the end, it was Prime Minister Mark Carney who emerged, among current politicians, as the strongest voice for staying in Canada.

[Read: As Alberta Rejects Separatism, Carney Gets Much of the Credit]

[Read In Opinion: Canada Said No, Again]

Similarly before the vote, Mitch Sylvestre, one of the most prominent separatist leaders, was equally unhappy with Ms. Smith.

“She’s playing a very interesting game that I think has very dire consequences for her,” he told me.

So where does that leave Ms. Smith?

Two days after the vote, she laid down the law around supporting Canada for her caucus and party members.

“For those few who cannot reconcile this fact and remain intent on dividing and turning our party into a vehicle for the independence movement, I would respectfully invite them to join a different party,” Ms. Smith said.

Again, the result angered the separatists, while many federalists complained that the gesture came too late.

At the end of November, the United Conservative Party will meet in the convention hall in Calgary where Mr. Carney gave a rousing and well-received speech to remain in Canada last week. Lisa Young, a political scientist at the University of Calgary, told me that it is now anybody’s guess what will happen to Ms. Smith and the party that was the result of a merger, in 2017, between the Progressive Conservatives and the Wildrose Party, which Ms. Smith once led.

“It’s incredibly puzzling,” Professor Young told me. “I keep trying to think about what she thought was going to happen the day after the vote. You’ve got to think that she just didn’t see this coming — that people would be angry at her for the referendum in the broader electorate.”

By gradually gaining control of local United Conservative riding or constituency associations, the separatists ousted Jason Kenney, the former federal Conservative cabinet minister, as the United Conservative Party leader and premier, and brought in Ms. Smith.

Professor Young said that it’s likely that the cabinet will back Ms. Smith.

“They want to keep their jobs,” Professor Young said. “There’s nobody plausible in the conservative movement who’s a better political communicator than she is.”

Also, Professor Young added, many U.C.P. members are aware that division and turmoil within their party can only benefit the New Democrats, who are currently led by Naheed Nenshi, the popular former mayor of Calgary.

“I would guess that they’re going to, sort of, reluctantly line up behind her, but that’s just a guess,” she said.

Further undermining Ms. Smith are the results of her nine other questions in the referendum.

Five of them passed by only small margins. Four of them were rejected.

An effective challenge next month to Ms. Smith from conservatives who were put off by the referendum and her other nine questions, Professor Young said, seems a remote possibility. That group has no obvious leader and many of them have given up on the party, she said.

“The people who have shown up for the last couple of years are essentially the separatists and others who are part of that right populist movement that got her in,” Professor Young said. “Everyone else has walked away.”

The monthslong referendum campaign revealed that the separatist movement is divided into several camps with differing concepts about an independent Alberta. That makes it difficult to predict what independence supporters who aren’t elected politicians will do in November.

“They just really love the protest life,” Professor Young said. “So they’re having the time of their lives. Why wouldn’t they keep it going?”

A fierce burst of wind inflamed a grass fire and raced about a kilometer in less than a minute toward a group of soldiers training at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta. Four of the people caught in the deadly onrush of flame died, and 39 were injured.

In the trade war, President Trump on Friday lifted some tariffs on Canadian products used by American farmers, ahead of the U.S. midterm elections. Earlier in the week, a group asked a court to strike down Mr. Trump’s steep tariffs, brought under a law from 1930, on Canadian products, arguing that the president had overstepped its provisions. And Pete Wells, who writes about food culture for The Times, reports that artisanal Canadian cheese was about to become a big deal in the United States — then the tariffs hit.

In Opinion, Chrystia Freeland, the former deputy prime minister, appeared on “The Ezra Klein show.”

Les Éditions du Boréal, the Quebec publisher, said it would not reprint “It Was Either That or Die,” or any other books by Thélyson Orélien, after finding evidence of A.I. use in early versions of the manuscript.

A man from Ontario was convicted in the birdnapping of Peachy, a flamingo at a Las Vegas casino hotel. He estimated that he had consumed 30 to 40 beers before committing the crime.

After a string of professional and romantic setbacks, Bayleigh Regina Pelham, who is originally from Halifax, found love with Stephanie Cassano of Toronto on a trip to Mexico.

Ian Austen reports on Canada for The Times. A Windsor, Ontario, native now based in Ottawa, he has reported on the country for two decades. He can be reached at austen@nytimes.com.

How are we doing?We’re eager to have your thoughts about this newsletter and events in Canada in general. Please send them to nytcanada@nytimes.com.

item.title: Paris, Battened Down Against Riots, Offers Lonely Welcome to Visitors
item.description:
A locked-down Paris is a headache for locals. But it was a heartache on Saturday for first-time visitors from Louisiana, who traveled here for an N.F.L. football game between the New Orleans Saints and Pittsburgh Steelers and found the Louvre museum closed and the Arc de Triomphe ringed by police vans.

“Just about everything is closed,” said Terri Wallis, 65, a school principal and Saints fan from Baton Rouge, who was visiting with three generations of her family. “You know, we’re not wealthy people. This is a once-in-a-lifetime trip to come and see the Mona Lisa. So, this is a little disappointing.”

The French authorities deployed as many as 70,000 police officers and gendarmes to prevent a repeat of last weekend, when mass protests degenerated into arson, looting and other violence. Officials in Paris and other cities hard hit by the unrest enforced curfews and temporary restrictions on gatherings.

In Paris, fears of another outbreak of violence prompted several cultural institutions, including the Louvre, Grand Palais, Orsay, Orangerie and Picasso museums, to close.

Ms. Wallis and her family were kicking around in a food store on the Avenue des Champs-Élysées, the city’s grandest boulevard, where traffic was light and private security guards were posted at most businesses’ entrances. All along the street, shops and boutiques were boarded up to protect them from looters.

With major cultural sites closed, Paris felt less chaotic than battened-down on a slate-gray Saturday afternoon. At the Louvre, a chain stretched across the door at the museum’s pyramid entrance. The Tuileries Gardens were also closed — because of high winds, a sign said.

While Notre-Dame Cathedral was open, Ms. Wallis said the lines outside it were extremely long, as tourists flocked to one of their few remaining options.

A midday bicycle ride through Paris revealed an eerily empty city. The Place de la Bastille, famous as the site of uprisings during the French Revolution and more recently the locus for student-led protests, had been ruled off-limits to demonstrators by the Paris authorities on Saturday.

A police phalanx, backed by a water-cannon truck and officers on motorcycles, kept the square clear. The police warned over a loudspeaker that anyone who tried to organize an illegal protest would be fined 135 euros, about $150.

“It’s not possible to stay here regardless of why you are here,” the voice on the loudspeaker said. “I ask you to leave the square.”

The authorities pushed the protesters to the southern periphery of the city, a last-minute change in the approved route for the march, which the organizers said was calculated to sow disarray in their ranks. Whether it would avert a repeat of the arson and looting that broke out across Paris last weekend was not yet clear.

Ms. Wallis said she considered calling off the trip after seeing those riots. But the Saints-Steelers game, the first N.F.L. match ever played in Paris, will go ahead as scheduled on Sunday in the Stade de France, a stadium in the Paris suburbs a few miles from where the high school protest movement began last month.

In those demonstrations, students erected barricades in front of their schools to protest dilapidated buildings, a shortage of teachers and a university admissions process that many say is opaque and unfair.

Chelsea Bertrand, who was with the Wallis family and works at an elementary school in Baton Rouge, said that as an educator, she was impressed by how the French students had mobilized, even if it affected her visit.

“You teach them to speak up for what’s right,” she said. “The fact that they’re actually standing up in a positive way — how it originally started — for their rights and what they think is best for education — I think that’s amazing.”

The women said they hadn’t witnessed any unrest and weren’t worried about their safety. Ms. Wallis said marveled at how “nonchalant” some people appeared to be about the disorder, pointing to a viral video on social media that appeared to show a couple relaxing in a cafe last weekend while fires burned outside.

“I thought, ‘OK, that’s the French,’” Ms. Wallis said. “The city’s burning and y’all are just sitting there.”

item.title: North Korea’s Kim Jong-un Arrives in China, South Korea Says
item.description:
North Korea’s leader, Kim Jong-un, crossed a new bridge into China on Saturday in his first visit to the neighboring country in more than a year, according to a South Korean government source and South Korean media.

The reason for the reported trip was unclear, but it comes as Beijing and Pyongyang deepen economic and strategic ties despite heavy international sanctions against North Korea. This evolving partnership was highlighted by the opening of the New Yalu River Bridge, which is the largest border crossing connecting the two countries, earlier this month.

Sunday also marks 76 years since Mao Zedong sent his forces into North Korea to support the embattled communist forces during the Korean War against an American-led United Nations coalition. Beijing hopes to promote relations with North Korea to “new heights,” China’s ambassador to North Korea, Wang Yajun, said at a commemorative event this week, China’s flagship newspaper reported.

Mr. Kim arrived in the Chinese city of Dandong, a hub for travel and commerce with North Korea, via the new bridge, according to the South Korean source, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because of the diplomatic sensitivity of the matter. South Korean news media also reported the trip, similarly citing anonymous government officials.

Dandong features a large museum commemorating the military ties forged between the two nations during the war.

The trip was not immediately confirmed by Beijing or Pyongyang.

South Korea keeps a constant eye on the movements of Mr. Kim, and its officials have sometimes announced Mr. Kim’s past visits to China first.

A public appearance by Mr. Kim would help dispel recent social media rumors of his death, which South Korean intelligence officials had already dismissed as false.

When Mr. Kim has visited China in the past, he has held talks with its top leader, Xi Jinping. But if or when the two might meet this time was unclear. From Monday, Mr. Xi will preside over a four-day meeting of the Chinese Communist Party’s Central Committee, an assembly of around 300 senior officials, in Beijing.

Posts on Chinese social media showed traffic snarls in Dandong, and some said residential compounds in the city had been sealed off to prevent people leaving. The area around Wanda Plaza, a commercial hub in Dandong, was blocked, with neither vehicles nor pedestrians allowed to pass, according to other posts. One user of Douyin, a Chinese social media service, shared a picture of North Korean and Chinese flags along a road in what the user said was Dandong.

Yonhap, South Korea’s main news agency, shared its report that Mr. Kim was visiting China on Weibo, a Chinese social media platform, with no interference — at least not immediately — from Chinese censors.

There has been speculation among diplomats and analysts that Mr. Kim might attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders’ meeting in Shenzhen, southern China, next month, though it is not clear if China has invited him.

President Trump, who has repeatedly expressed his eagerness to resume personal diplomacy with Mr. Kim, has said he will attend that meeting.

Mr. Kim is also trying to deepen ties with Russia. North Korea has provided Russia with critical artillery shells, missiles and troops for its war in Ukraine, prompting Moscow to sign a mutual defense treaty and supply the North with food, oil, and advanced military technology.

In response, Mr. Xi has moved to reassert Beijing’s influence. He invited both Mr. Kim and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia to a military parade in Beijing last September. Rail service between Beijing and Pyongyang, suspended during the Covid pandemic, resumed in March, and Mr. Xi visited Pyongyang in June.

Bilateral trade has expanded rapidly. Decades of international sanctions have left North Korea reliant on China for nearly all of its external trade.

Mr. Kim’s first visit to China, and first trip abroad as North Korea’s leader was in 2018. Since then, Mr. Kim has traveled to China several times, holding talks with Mr. Xi each time. On his most recent visit last year, he attended a military parade in Beijing to mark 80 years since the end of World War II.

Murphy Zhao contributed reporting from Hong Kong.

item.title: Netanyahu Has Reinvented Himself. Will Voters Think It’s Enough?
item.description:
Benjamin Netanyahu looks thinner and paler these days. Gone is the swagger of previous political campaigns. But he remains tireless, traipsing among shopping centers and television studios, trying to persuade a weary and polarized country to return him to office for up to another four years in Israeli elections on Tuesday.

At 77, he is already Israel’s longest-serving prime minister. If he is to extend that tenure, he has to sell the deeply divided electorate on the new, more hawkish version of himself — and of Israel.

Mr. Netanyahu’s career will forever be defined by the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel, the deadliest day for Jews since the Holocaust. He long had a reputation for being risk averse and avoiding military confrontations, even as he cultivated an image as Israel’s Mr. Security. But that image, as well as Israel’s confidence in its own defense, was badly damaged that day.

So Mr. Netanyahu, known by friends and foes as Bibi, reinvented himself. Instead of sticking to Israel’s previous security doctrine centered on short wars of defense, he has waged Israel’s longest war on multiple fronts — against Hamas in Gaza, Hezbollah militants in Lebanon, the Houthi militia in Yemen and, together with the United States, Iran.

He has doubled down on Israel’s occupation of the West Bank, allowing Jewish settlements to proliferate and settler violence against Palestinians to escalate, further aggravating Israel’s international isolation.

“He understood that if he wanted to survive, not only politically but as a historic figure, he had to change,” said Mazal Mualem, an Israeli political commentator and Netanyahu biographer. “He killed off the old Bibi and delivered a new one into the world,” she added.

After the Oct. 7 attacks, Mr. Netanyahu promised total victory over Hamas and other enemies. While Israel’s military campaign has left those adversaries battered, the wars have been inconclusive. Now, he says there is more to be done, and that he is the one to do it. “We must complete the elimination of the Iranian regime,” he said on Tuesday.

It is unclear whether he will get the chance. Days before what many Israelis view as the most fateful election in the country’s history, Mr. Netanyahu and his Likud party are in a tight race against an opposition led by Gadi Eisenkot, a centrist and former military chief. Opinion polls show the opposition slightly ahead but lacking enough seats to guarantee a governing coalition.

Mr. Netanyahu may have lost some of his luster, but he is a master politician who has maintained a loyal base of supporters and cultivated strong political alliances, meaning that he cannot be counted out.

As prime minister for most of the past 17 years, in addition to a three-year term in the 1990s, Mr. Netanyahu has evolved along with the Israel he has largely shaped.

He returned to power in late 2022 after a brief hiatus. Shunned by other mainstream parties because he faces corruption charges, Mr. Netanyahu formed a governing coalition with the participation of far-right extremists who had been considered beyond the pale by most Israeli politicians.

At the time, he told Israel’s Parliament that the country was in its “golden age” after “the quietest and safest security decade in our history.” Even as he repeated a pledge to block Iran from developing a nuclear weapon, he trumpeted his aim to “widen the circle of peace” with the goal of ending the Arab-Israeli conflict.

Instead, on the morning of Oct. 7, 2023, thousands of gunmen surged across the border from Gaza, overrunning Israeli communities, army bases and a music festival, killing about 1,200 people, according to the Israeli authorities, and taking 251 hostages.

Mr. Netanyahu has not taken personal responsibility for government failures that preceded the attacks, including his policy aimed at fostering quiet in Hamas-run Gaza rather than confronting the militant group, or the military and intelligence lapses that left Israel vulnerable. He has blocked an independent state inquiry into what went wrong.

Mr. Netanyahu says that his security chiefs chose not to wake him on Oct. 7.

But Mr. Netanyahu and Israeli security leaders repeatedly downplayed signs that Gaza militants were gearing up for an assault, including reports of heightened Hamas activity from female military spotters and the acquisition of a Hamas battle plan.

Israel’s war against Hamas killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, according to Gaza health officials, prompting accusations of war crimes against Mr. Netanyahu from rights groups and foreign governments.

Critics and former Israeli officials also say he prolonged the war in Gaza, which Israel launched in response to the Oct. 7 attacks, and delayed deals for the release of hostages — to keep his far-right coalition partners on board and remain in power. The prime minister’s office did not respond to a request for comment.

The wars have also overstretched the military and taken a toll on many Israelis, who have performed repeated tours as reserve soldiers. At the same time, Mr. Netanyahu has extended the exemption of ultra-Orthodox Jewish men from mandatory military service, bending to the demands of his ultra-Orthodox coalition partners who say religious study is a higher priority.

Israel’s conduct in the Gaza war has also left the country increasingly isolated and facing international boycotts and embargoes. Although Mr. Netanyahu, who spent part of his childhood in Pennsylvania, prides himself on speaking “American,” support for Israel in the United States is at an unprecedented low, said Daniel B. Shapiro, a former U.S. ambassador to Israel.

“There’s no way you could reverse that without a change in leadership, in the face of Israel,” he added.

Mr. Netanyahu’s vision of an Israeli Sparta — an insular, self-sufficient, militaristic society — which he offered at an economic conference in 2025, has been deeply unsettling for many Israelis, who have traditionally enjoyed economic and other ties overseas.

In the past, Mr. Netanyahu was loath to preside over an open-ended war. “I am not eager for unnecessary wars,” he said in 2018 amid tensions along the Gaza border, adding that he was working to ease the economic crisis in the enclave to prevent an escalation in violence.

For a quarter-century, mostly under Mr. Netanyahu, Israel lived largely within its border fences after withdrawing from southern Lebanon in 2000 and from Gaza in 2005.

Now, saying it is acting to protect Israeli border communities, Israel is again occupying swaths of territory in Lebanon and Gaza, and expanded the area it occupies in Syria. Military policies of containment have been set aside. On Sunday, Mr. Netanyahu published his updated national security doctrine, putting a priority on pre-empting threats.

After Israel killed Hezbollah’s longtime leader in Lebanon, in 2024, Mr. Netanyahu summed up his philosophy by invoking a Talmudic teaching on pre-emptive action. “If someone rises up to kill you,” he said, “kill him first.”

On the campaign trail, Mr. Netanyahu continues to sound an alert about what he deems threats external and internal, stoking fear of Israel’s Arab citizens and questioning the legitimacy of the political parties that represent them.

On a recent weeknight, security officers ushered Mr. Netanyahu into a grimy food court at a shopping mall in Holon, a Tel Aviv suburb. About 200 people were waiting for him.

“Bibi, King of Israel!” the crowd chanted, repeating a common refrain.

Struggling to be heard over an inadequate sound system, Mr. Netanyahu delivered a stump speech of barely 90 seconds.

“Do you want Mansour Abbas?” he asked, referring to the leader of an Arab political party that could play kingmaker in a close election.

“No!” the crowd cried.

“Well go out and vote Likud!” he exhorted, before being whisked away.

“I love him,” said Shimon Karni, 48, who was in the crowd. “I’m proud of what he’s done for Israel and the Jewish people,” he said. “May he be our prime minister till he’s 120.”

Mr. Netanyahu’s supporters call him a unique leader.

“The prime minister is a proud Israeli patriot who believes with every fiber of his being that he is the only leader capable of dealing with the challenges facing Israel,” said Ofer Golan, a former adviser to Mr. Netanyahu. “And I believe he is right.”

Since the last election, Mr. Netanyahu and his allies have also begun to target what they call enemies in the deep state, including Israel’s attorney general and top judges.

This transformation of Mr. Netanyahu began long before the Oct. 7 attacks, analysts say, dating it to 2019, when he was indicted on charges of bribery, fraud and breach of trust in three separate but related corruption cases. On trial since 2020, he has denied any wrongdoing and accused the deep state of trying to oust him through a judicial putsch after failing at the ballot box.

Mr. Netanyahu once pointed to Israel’s democratic institutions as a beacon in the Middle East. After he was indicted, “he perceived the legal apparatus as a direct foe,” said Yohanan Plesner, the president of the Israel Democracy Institute, a nonpartisan research group.

In January 2023, Mr. Netanyahu’s justice minister, Yariv Levin, announced a plan for a sweeping judicial overhaul. Mr. Netanyahu said it was necessary to rein in what he called an overactive judiciary, restore the balance between the branches of government and give more power to elected officials.

Opponents of the plan said the proposed measures would remove checks on government power and lead to a dictatorship of the majority. Mass protests erupted across the country. Some Israelis feared a civil war. Israel’s security chiefs said they warned repeatedly that the protests and social schism weakened Israel in the eyes of its enemies and would lead to war.

Mr. Netanyahu’s critics say he became engrossed in his personal troubles and surrounded himself with a shrinking coterie of loyalists.

“He was of course a man of many capabilities, but more important, he had a detailed strategic vision,” said Ehud Yaari, an Israel-based fellow of the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. His aims included developing relations with African nations and expanding agreements with Arab Gulf states.

“But instead of focusing on the big goals, he began his personal war,” Mr. Yaari said. “It was a different Netanyahu, with different priorities. His attention drifted elsewhere.”

For years, Mr. Netanyahu pursued formal relations with moderate Arab Gulf states to bypass Palestinians or pressure them into greater territorial compromise. After the Abraham Accords of 2020 normalized Israel’s relations with Morocco, Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates, the big prize was to be Saudi Arabia.

But Mr. Netanyahu’s far-right partners prevented him from proposing an eventual pathway to Palestinian statehood as the Saudi government demanded. In the past, he had paid lip service, at least, to the idea of a demilitarized Palestinian state.

“To preserve his coalition, he gave up on that too,” said Gayil Talshir, a political scientist at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

Instead, he has proceeded in lock step with members of his government seeking to eventually annex the West Bank. His policies there, together with his failure to tackle mounting violence by Israeli settlers against Palestinians, contributed to the recent imposition of sanctions by several countries once among Israel’s staunchest allies.

“We all wonder where his head is at, where his personal value system is,” said Shalom Lipner, another former aide to several Israeli leaders, including Mr. Netanyahu. He added, “We’ve seen him shift to be able to stay in the chair.”

item.title: Violent Protests Resurface in Albania: What to Know
item.description:
Thousands of people marched Saturday through Albania’s capital, where student protests over the costs of education have swelled into broader discontent with the government.

Two weeks ago, the student protest joined with months of demonstrations over the cost of living and calls for Prime Minister Edi Rama to step down. But protests quickly turned violent in Tirana, the capital, before spreading to other Albanian cities.

On Saturday, demonstrators returned to Tirana’s main boulevard and marched through the city. The building housing the Environment Ministry went up in flames after Molotov cocktails were lobbed through its doors, according to a local news report. The police tried to disperse the crowd with water cannons and tear gas.

Instead, the protesters changed course toward the headquarters of the governing Socialist Party near Skanderbeg Square in central Tirana. There, they clashed with police officers in riot gear guarding the building.

Across the country 283 people have been arrested and 363 charged since this month’s protests began, officials said.

The students have vowed to keep demonstrating and have rebuffed the prime minister’s invitation to talk. Mr. Rama, for his part, has refused to step down and said the students’ legitimate concerns have been overtaken by his political opponents.

Here’s what you need to know.

The protests kicked off on Oct. 13 in support of peaceful demonstrations already underway against a planned luxury development linked to Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law.

“After more than 130 days of a national peaceful protest, we, as students, wanted to show that we have many other reasons to protest,” Emir Lecini, a member of the student group that helped start the movement, said. “Our system of education is unacceptable, cost of living is high and students are not treated with dignity.”

Prime Minister Rama, who has been in office for 13 years and in and out of the Albanian government since 1998, has been the main target of the anger, and protesters are demanding his resignation.

“I’m protesting because I want Albania to be a country that is not ruled like a dictatorship,” said Redjan Shkembi, 22, a recent university graduate, who first joined the demonstrations against the Kushner-linked development. As the protests in Albania grew, he saw it as part of wider student-led movements in France, Spain and elsewhere.

“We feel connected to the youth protests we are seeing across Europe,” he said.

Refusing to resign, Mr. Rama has said the students’ legitimate calls for change have been overshadowed by groups seeking to derail Albania’s plans to join the European Union, one of his administration’s main objectives.

On social media, he has invited the students to a dialogue and posted videos of empty chairs. He has also urged them to distance themselves from the groups he said were encouraging violence.

“Peaceful protest is a democratic value,” Mr. Rama said in a video posted to Facebook on Saturday. “Violence at a protest is a social ill and a criminal challenge to the state, the law and public safety. It cannot be tolerated or justified.”

Last week, in a video from a looted shop, he also announced a new online platform where businesses damaged in the unrest could apply for compensation.

Images of the police responding to the student protests with force have also provoked public anger. Last week, Albania’s national police suspended two officers who were recorded on video pushing a student, who local news outlets said sustained a spinal fracture in the incident.

The police said they had since suspended more officers for excessive force.

Public discontent in Albania initially coalesced around a proposed luxury development linked to Mr. Kushner, his wife, Ivanka Trump and investors in the Persian Gulf.

The coastal development, expected to cost more than $4 billion, was approved soon after Mr. Trump began his second term and developers promoted it as a major tourism investment. But environmental groups in Albania opposed construction near the village of Zvernec and the largely uninhabited island, Sazan.

The protests began after a video circulated online: It showed private security guards on May 30 dragging away a man who had joined a few dozen residents and environmental activists on a beach in southern Albania that Mr. Kushner and his business partners want to be part of the proposed hotel and resort. Dubbed the “flamingo revolution,” a nod to the region’s rich bird life, the protests had until recently been largely peaceful, resembling a nightly carnival in Tirana.

Mr. Rama said last month that the development was on hold while the government assessed how it would affect the surrounding environment. Whether construction on the luxury project will proceed depends on the assessment, he said.

item.title: Why Is the U.S. Accusing Canada of Election Interference?
item.description:
As President Trump stares down what could be a bruising midterm election in November for the Republican Party amid his record-low approval ratings, his administration has identified a familiar target to place some blame: Canada.

This past week, the U.S. Embassy in Ottawa said Canada’s “ministers and premiers openly describe plans to influence American politics in official documents and public appearances.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada said in a news conference on Friday that those claims had “no merit” and that his government was ready to “drop everything” to negotiate an end to its costly trade war with the United States.

The Trump administration’s claims of election interference added to a long list of animosities that have been piling up between the two countries since Mr. Trump’s second term began.

In a statement on Wednesday, the U.S. Embassy accused Canadian officials of meeting with Democratic lawmakers, urging the use of retaliatory levies to hit Republican states and running anti-tariff political advertising campaigns in the United States.

The embassy zeroed in on Canada’s industry minister, Mélanie Joly, who has said or implied on multiple occasions that her nation’s trade policy was designed to strategically hit Republican states. In a news conference in August, shortly after trade talks had collapsed, Ms. Joly said Canada would impose tariffs on “products that will target states in the U.S.” to “put political pressure” on the Trump administration.

The embassy also said she met in September with Democratic officials in Boston and Chicago. Ms. Joly said the goal of the trip was to discuss trade and investments with individual U.S. states and companies.

In addition, the embassy’s statement recalled an incident in October of last year in which Doug Ford, Ontario’s conservative premier, announced he would run an advertisement that included sound bites of President Ronald Reagan criticizing tariffs. In response, the Trump administration halted trade negotiations altogether.

Pete Hoekstra, the U.S. ambassador to Canada, has since walked back his office’s accusations.

“Someone could assume” based on Canadian officials’ actions that they were trying to interfere in U.S. elections, Mr. Hoekstra said on a Canadian politics podcast recorded on Wednesday and released Friday. “As an embassy, we hadn’t reached that conclusion.”

Mr. Trump has repeatedly drawn Canadians’ ire by calling the nation America’s “51st state,” and by moving to rename Lake Ontario, which straddles the border between the two countries, “Lake America.”

But the greatest strain on the neighbors’ relationship has been their trade war. Shortly after President Trump returned to office, he imposed tariffs on Canadian exports in return for what he said was the country’s role in allowing fentanyl to enter the United States. Canada retaliated with tariffs of its own, and the dispute has devolved into an ongoing retaliation hurting businesses and consumers in both countries.

On Friday, the Trump administration announced that it would shuffle its tariffs on Canadian products, exempting some items and applying new tariffs to others, in what appeared to be a last-minute bid to provide relief to American farmers ahead of the midterm elections.

At a news conference in Turkey on Friday, Mr. Carney said Canada took pains to avoid the appearance of meddling in U.S. politics. And he dismissed any notion that Canadian officials had favored one party or another in its dealings.

“We have no intention to interfere with their democratic processes,” he said.

Ms. Joly also defended herself against the U.S. Embassy’s claims on Thursday. “Indeed, I met with Democrats in the U.S., but I met with Republicans,” as well, she said.

On Wednesday, Mr. Ford told reporters he had “no interest” in engaging in election interference.

“We’re going to focus on what we can do here in Ontario, and in Canada, to make sure we protect our economy, protect the people and protect communities,” he said. “And the people of the United States will make that determination in the midterms.”

Stewart Prest, a political science lecturer at the University of British Columbia, said the Canadian actions cited by the U.S. Embassy could have been intended to encourage policy changes, not to hurt Republicans at the ballot box.

In his statements, Mr. Carney noted that some Trump administration officials met with Albertan separatists this year, before the province’s referendum on holding a vote on whether to secede from Canada. (Voters roundly rejected it.)

“The resources of the media here can make their own judgment about the extent to which very, very senior U.S. officials have directly intervened, so to speak, in Canadian sovereignty, Canadian democratic processes,” Mr. Carney said.

White House and State Department officials confirmed that State Department officials met with activists in the separatist movement in Washington three times last year. But the Trump administration has denied making any material promises to Albertan separatists.

“The department regularly meets with civil society types,” the State Department said in a statement. “As is typical in routine meetings such as these, no commitments were made.”

To Mr. Prest, the political science lecturer, the Trump administration’s rhetoric and involvement in the Albertan separatist movement showed that its latest claims of election interference by Canada smacked of hypocrisy.

“The accusation is itself a kind of confession,” he said. The administration was “trying to create an equivalency where I don’t think any exists.”

item.title: Israel Launches Crackdown in West Bank City After Deadly Attack
item.description:
The Israeli military said it had launched a sweeping crackdown in the West Bank city of Hebron overnight after Palestinian gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers there and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu vowed to retaliate days before a pivotal election.

Residents of Hebron, the largest Palestinian city in the Israeli-occupied territory, said on Saturday that Israeli troops had erected roadblocks and closed the main entrances and exits to the city.

Israeli forces have started demolishing structures close to the scene of the attack, the military said, adding that the operation in the area would last for several days. Residents would be allowed to leave through designated checkpoints. An Israeli military spokesman did not respond to a request for comment on whether they would be allowed to return home.

The worsening violence in the West Bank came days before an important Israeli election, the first since the Hamas-led attacks of Oct. 7, 2023, that ignited the devastating war in Gaza. Mr. Netanyahu is fighting for his political life and has trailed his leading opponent, Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief, in opinion polls throughout the campaign.

On Friday, two Palestinians opened fire on Israeli troops near a checkpoint in Hebron, killing two soldiers before being shot dead, according to the Israeli military. Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir, the Israeli military chief of staff, said in a statement that the soldiers had prevented “an even more serious attack.” The military said a large cache of ammunition was found in a vehicle used by the attackers.

Mr. Netanyahu visited the scene of the attacks on Friday and vowed a broad crackdown in the West Bank, including by imposing a security cordon around Hebron and a lockdown of the territory. Israeli forces would also search the homes of residents, he added.

“We are acting, first of all, to destroy this place, to utterly change it,” Mr. Netanyahu said.

Some Israeli analysts have expressed concern that the prime minister’s decision to start a major military operation might be influenced by the election. Mr. Netanyahu has sought to burnish his security credentials to Israeli voters rattled by three years of constant war.

It was unclear whether the shooters acted alone or on behalf of a Palestinian militant group. Hamas, the Palestinian armed group based in Gaza, praised the attack but stopped short of claiming responsibility for it.

The attacks took place against a backdrop of rising violence in the West Bank since the Oct. 7 attacks. In recent weeks, extremist Jewish settlers have initiated dozens of attacks against Palestinians during the annual olive harvest, a cultural touchstone for many Palestinians. Masked Israelis have assaulted Palestinian olive gatherers, beating them with clubs and hurling stones.

Since early last year, the Israeli military has been conducting a wide crackdown, displacing tens of thousands of people and destroying roads and houses, in what it said was an effort to target militants.

Last month, an Israeli man was shot dead in the West Bank, according to the Israeli authorities, who said they had detained a Palestinian suspect in connection with the attack.

item.title: ‘Eagle’s Nest,’ Nazi-Era Guesthouse in German Alps, Is Gutted by Fire
item.description:
An enormous fire all but destroyed an infamous Nazi-era guesthouse known as the Eagle’s Nest in southern Germany, according to the police, who said on Saturday that a man had been arrested in connection with the blaze.

The fire started on Friday night, the authorities said, and firefighters worked overnight to try to save the historic structure, which sits at an altitude of about 6,000 feet, just below a peak in southern Bavaria. No one was hurt, the authorities said.

The police said on Saturday morning that the building, formally known as the Kehlsteinhaus, was probably not salvageable. They gave no details about the man who had been arrested, saying that their investigation into the fire and whether it had been deliberately set was continuing.

The Kehlsteinhaus — completed in 1938, well into Hitler’s regime — was built as a guesthouse for high-ranking Nazi officials and their visitors. It was about three miles from Hitler’s alpine residence.

After Germany’s defeat in World War II, the Bavarian state government wanted to tear it down, but local officials fought successfully to keep it, seeing it as a historical site that could attract visitors.

The house is surrounded by rough mountainous terrain near the Austrian border. Tourists took buses through a series of tunnels to reach the base of the last knoll, then took an elevator to the guesthouse, which had panoramic views of the German Alps.

On Friday, the house and its accompanied restaurant were closed, which is one reason the police were confident that no one had been hurt. A fire alarm sounded in the nearby town of Berchtesgaden at 9:15 p.m., officials said.

By 9:52 p.m., when the first fire trucks reached the site, the guesthouse was engulfed in flames, according to the authorities.

item.title: Speed of Starshield Satellite Network Is Improving, Ukraine Says
item.description:
Ukrainian drones connected to the Pentagon-funded Starshield satellite network have flown at speeds near 250 miles an hour for the first time since the system was throttled last week, Ukraine’s defense minister announced on Saturday. It was the first sign that the speed restrictions, which have hampered crucial drone operations, might be easing.

“This is another example when direct dialogue and the persistent position of the president of Ukraine at the highest level produce results,” Yevhen Khmara, the defense minister, said in a statement. “And this result is primarily important for our front, for the military, the work of drones, logistics and communications.”

Ukraine uses Starshield for air defense and to guide drones toward targets in Russian-occupied territory. The unexplained throttling of the system deepened a growing rift that has been playing out publicly between Ukraine and the United States. President Volodymyr Zelensky warned that Ukrainian civilians had been left more vulnerable to Russian attack, and Ukrainian officials raised fears that the Starshield program had been slowed to force Ukraine into capitulation.

Ukrainian drone operators first saw their drones slowed to speeds lower than 40 miles an hour about 10 days ago. Many drones slowed so abruptly that they lost connection to their pilots on the ground and then fell from the sky, wasting expensive equipment.

It remains unclear who, if anyone, ordered the system to be slowed. No one in Washington has taken responsibility, a fact that only caused further confusion in Kyiv.It has also deepened divides between Congress and the White House over the U.S. approach to Russia. A group of Republicans and Democrats in the Senate warned the White House this week that they would block President Trump’s nominations if Ukraine’s full Starshield capabilities were not restored.
